title: The Consilience Doughnut: scale, engagement and what the record of knowledge integration leaves out

detail.title: The Consilience Doughnut: scale, engagement and what the record of knowledge integration leaves out

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Two axes organise knowledge in environmental governance: spatio-temporal scale, from the individual to the global, and engagement, from knowledge co-constituted by the communities it concerns (in vivo) to knowledge produced under researcher-controlled conditions (in vitro). We argue that both have closed — social network services joining the individual to the global directly, and large language models supplying access to the in vitro pole without the institution that formerly granted it, the second of these argued here without measurement — so that the surface they define is a torus, the Consilience Doughnut, on which every position is in principle occupiable. Where documents actually sit is a separate question. A four-point rubric, fixed before the evidence, was applied unchanged to 2,223 paragraphs from three independently assembled corpora: eleven assessment, methodology and case-study documents, three transnational economic-governance bodies in two genres, and Future Earth. The formalised band holds 69.0% of all paragraphs and the contextual band 1.0%. No document reaches the deliberative rung on average, and the two documents reporting structured public deliberation are a full engagement rung apart. Position on the engagement axis is a property of the text and not of the process the text describes: the record of knowledge integration is written in the institutional register. Agricultural carbon crediting shows the mechanism in an operating market, where the verifier admits auditable dates and excludes the judgement that reads a field. The second closure places the translation between the poles in the hands of models trained at one of them.

title: When Accuracy Saturates, Reliability Leads: A Staged Evaluation of Uncertainty Estimators for 3D Pancreas Segmentation
affiliations: Université de Moncton, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Hail, Alfaisal University and Université de Moncton

detail.title: When Accuracy Saturates, Reliability Leads: A Staged Evaluation of Uncertainty Estimators for 3D Pancreas Segmentation

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Architectural innovation on three-dimensional medical image segmentation increasingly yieldsdiminishing returns: on well-posed tasks a competent backbone already recovers most of theavailable spatial signal, so accuracy saturates and additional modules move it little. We arguethat in this regime the actionable axis is reliability rather than accuracy, and we test this claimthrough a staged protocol grounded in the Unified Variational Intelligence Framework (UVIF),whose uncertainty term becomes the natural target once the task loss plateaus. On the MedicalSegmentation Decathlon pancreas task (281 CT volumes; pancreas and mass classes), Stage 1establishes saturation: under a controlled multi-seed protocol with a fixed held-out test set andHolm-corrected paired tests, neither a learnable Fourier band-pass module, a learnable Fresnelpropagationmodule, nor an edge-attention reference improves Dice over a plain residual U-Net.Stage 2 reuses the trained models, without retraining, to evaluate five uncertainty estimators asfailure detectors. Deep-ensemble disagreement is significantly better calibrated and more reliablethan single-model confidence (failure-detectionAUROC 0.80 vs. 0.74; expected calibration error0.075 vs. 0.156; all 𝑝 < 10−4). In contrast, two physics-motivated single-pass estimators derivedfrom Fresnel diffraction—feature-space coherence and decision-space view-disagreement—underperform even trivial softmax entropy. We conclude that ensembling, not architectural orsingle-pass physics priors, delivers reliable uncertainty on accuracy-saturated segmentation, andthat ensemble disagreement furnishes a concrete estimator for the UVIF uncertainty term.

title: What you don’t see, you don’t get? Understanding societal support for climate and nitrogen reduction policies
affiliations: Radboud University, PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (The Hague), Radboud University, Radboud University and Radboud University

detail.title: What you don’t see, you don’t get? Understanding societal support for climate and nitrogen reduction policies

affiliations.org_name: PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (The Hague)
affiliations.preferred_name: PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (The Hague)

detail.abstract: Societal support for environmental policies is decreasing as politicization has polarized the debate. For climate policy this has been well-studied, but not for nitrogen policies, which are becoming more salient in Europe. This study aims to fill this gap and examines the relationship between environmental attitudes, political beliefs and public support for nitrogen reduction policies, comparing outcomes with what explains support for climate policy. The study analyses whether support is specific to the topic or rather driven by more generic factors. The study uses an innovative mixed-method design in three steps, combining clustering analysis, focus groups and regression analyses, using data from the National Election Survey (2023) from the Netherlands. Our main finding is that to a certain extent insights from the literature on climate policy support work fairly well in explaining nitrogen policy support. In particular, education and political affiliation play an important role. That being said, we also find that there are explanatory factors specific to support for nitrogen policy. Here, regional identity and the importance the respondent attaches to the trade-offs caused by policy interventions, like reduced housing construction projects or a smaller livestock sector, are more important. Overall the results suggest that indeed what people don’t see they don’t get, which makes acceptance of policies that cause tangible costs and trade-offs difficult when the gains are more intangible to grasp.

title: Green Investors in a Brown Market: Evidence from Ethereum’s Energy Transition
affiliations: Xiamen University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Green Investors in a Brown Market: Evidence from Ethereum’s Energy Transition

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Can green investment behavior emerge within a brown asset market? Before The Merge, all Ether was secured by the same energy-intensive Proof-of-Work network, yet its investors need not share the same environmental preferences. Using a daily panel of 20,012 accounts, we identify green preferences from responses to public attention to global warming before the event-study period. We then examine Ethereum’s September 2022 transition to Proof-of-Stake, which reduced the network’s electricity consumption and carbon footprint by over 99.9%. Accounts with stronger green preferences increase their net Ether purchases relative to other accounts after the transition. Crucially, green accounts’ larger pre-transition net outflows converge toward those of non-green accounts, consistent with the removal of a brown discount rather than the emergence of a green premium. Pre-transition differences in holding and selling gains also fade, suggesting that financial considerations accompany environmental preferences. The findings reveal green behavior inside an energy-intensive market and distinguish the lifting of a brown penalty from a new reward for greenness.

title: A framework for combined epidemiological-genomic inference to improve estimation of household model parameters
affiliations: The University of Manchester, The University of Manchester and The University of Manchester

detail.title: A framework for combined epidemiological-genomic inference to improve estimation of household model parameters
detail.abstract: Models incorporating household structure, with different rates oftransmission within and between households, are widely used in infectious diseaseepidemiology. These models can be calibrated using final-size data in whichtransmission ordering is ignored because it does not affect the distributionof final outbreak sizes. In particular, many distincttransmission histories produce identical final epidemiological outcomes,making it difficult to distinguish internal (within-household) from external(between-household) transmission and limiting parameter identifiability.Here, we develop a continuous-time Markov chain formulation for householdtransmission dynamics in which the model statespace is expanded to include transmission graphs describing infectiondirection and order, with idealised pathogen genomic data used to identifythe transmission histories compatible with observations.We conduct simulation studies which show that incorporating genetic informationsubstantially concentrates the regions of high likelihood compared with models basedon epidemiological data alone. In particular, genomic data reduces thedependence between internal and external transmission parameters,removing the characteristic ridge associated with their weak identifiability.These results demonstrate that graph-resolved household models enableimproved transmission inference while maintaining analytical andcomputational tractability.

title: Cross-Market Spillovers from City Gas Liberalization to Electricity Contract Switching in Japan
affiliations: Saitama University, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Saitama University and Guangdong Medical University

detail.title: Cross-Market Spillovers from City Gas Liberalization to Electricity Contract Switching in Japan

affiliations.org_name: Ishikawa Prefectural University - Department of Bioproduction Science
affiliations.preferred_name: Saitama University, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences

affiliations.org_name: Saitama University - Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences
affiliations.preferred_name: Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences

detail.abstract: Consumer inertia limits the gains from retail energy liberalization. This study asks whether Japan's April 2017 city gas retail liberalization changed outcomes in the electricity retail market that had opened one year earlier. A continuous-treatment difference-in-differences design is applied to a balanced monthly panel of 47 prefectures from April 2016 to March 2025, with pre-existing city gas penetration measuring exposure to the reform. After 2017, a prefecture with a 10-percentage-point higher penetration rate recorded an additional 1.75-percentage-point increase in the share of low-voltage demand supplied under free-rate electricity contracts. The number of electricity retailers did not rise with penetration, and the retailer-count coefficients are small and negative. The consumer-side result remains positive and significant when treatment values are capped at 100%, when Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto are excluded, and when electricity-area trends are added, and placebo tests on pre-reform dates find no comparable effects. This pattern fits an incumbent-led channel in which gas suppliers use their customer bases and dual-fuel bundles to move households onto free-rate contracts. Bundling can activate inactive consumers, and it can also raise acquisition costs for independent retailers and create dual-fuel lock-in. Because gas infrastructure is uneven, the gains concentrate in infrastructure-rich prefectures. Regulators can monitor price gaps between default and free-rate tariffs, cancellation fees on bundled contracts, and the market shares of multi-product incumbents, and they can support price-comparison tools and switching assistance in low-infrastructure regions. These measures bear on Sustainable Development Goal 7 (affordable and clean energy).

title: Integration without decentralization: the financial geography of U.S. life insurance, 1880 - 1940

detail.title: Integration without decentralization: the financial geography of U.S. life insurance, 1880 - 1940
detail.abstract: American life insurers were the largest institution for contractual saving in the United Statesbefore Social Security. This paper asks whether control over the savings they collected becamegeographically dispersed as the market for insurance became national. Using a newly digitizedannual panel of premiums and losses by firm and state for nearly every legal-reserve life insurerfrom 1888 to 1940, I separate the geography of collection, where premiums were paid, fromthe geography of control, the states in which the collecting firms were domiciled and madetheir underwriting, investment, and expansion decisions. The number of insurers rose from 56in 1890 to 359 in 1940, incorporation shifted toward the Midwest and South, and the medianwithin-state Herfindahl index fell by 52 percent. Yet the five largest firms collected 54 percentof national premium in 1890 and 53 percent in 1940, and the share collected by firms domiciledin the state of collection fell from 23.3 percent in the 1890s to 20.8 percent in the 1930s. Gainsin local retention came almost entirely from states acquiring their first domestic insurer, andthe Northeast–South gap in retention closed chiefly because the South rose. Local control rosesubstantially only where the law compelled it: after the Robertson Law of 1907, the in-stateshare of Texas premium rose from 7 to 60 percent within six years, as premium collected thereby out-of-state insurers fell by more than half relative to the rest of the South. Participationin legal-reserve insurance converged across states before 1920, in part through the decline offraternal insurance, and diverged thereafter.
